title: Deadly Nor'easter Pummels Northeast, Leaving Over 130,000 Without Power
snippet: A slow-moving weekend storm hammered the coastal Northeast with heavy rains, fierce winds, and tidal surges, causing widespread blackouts and at least one fatality.
content:
A relentless Nor'easter continued to batter the northeastern United States on Sunday, bringing destructive coastal flooding, heavy downpours, and damaging wind gusts to millions of residents. The storm has claimed at least one life and knocked out power to over 136,000 homes and businesses across the region.

Tragic Loss and Widespread Outages

The severe weather turned fatal in New York City on Saturday afternoon when a falling tree struck and killed a New York City Housing Authority worker in East New York, Brooklyn. Farther east, a scare off Fire Island ended relievedly after a missing swimmer safely reestablished contact with law enforcement Sunday morning.

As the storm dragged on, power outages escalated rapidly. According to tracking data from PowerOutage.us, utility crews were working to restore power to roughly 136,000 customers across New Jersey, New York, Connecticut, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island on Sunday—a sharp increase from 85,000 outages reported Saturday. Shoreline regions, including Long Island's Suffolk County and New Jersey's Ocean and Monmouth counties, were among the hardest hit by utility disruptions.

Soaking Rains and High Winds

The National Weather Service reported staggering rainfall totals across the eastern seaboard. Portions of southeastern Massachusetts recorded more than 6 inches of rain, while the northern Jersey Shore saw around 5 inches. Coupled with wind gusts peaking between 40 and 50 mph, high tides triggered minor to moderate coastal flooding along vulnerable waterfront areas.

Meteorologists expect the storm to gradually weaken through late Sunday afternoon before fully moving off the coast by Monday night.

Staying Safe in the Aftermath

Emergency management officials are emphasizing caution as floodwaters slowly recede. Residents in low-lying areas are urged to move vehicles to higher ground prior to high tide cycles. Authorities strongly advise against driving or walking through flooded roads, noting that as little as 6 inches of moving water can knock an adult off their feet. Any downed power lines should be treated as live and reported immediately to local utilities or 911.
